title: Isolated Acute Dysphagia as a Probable Rare Presentation of Guillain–Barré Syndrome with Complete Recovery: A Case Report
case_prompt: A 76-year-old woman presented with sudden-onset dysphagia during meals, characterized by difficulty swallowing, frequent aspirations, and nasal regurgitation when ingesting larger boluses. This was her second dysphagia episode; a similar transient episode 3 years earlier resolved spontaneously. Her medical history included a left posterior cerebral artery infarction 9 years ago without residual deficits. She denied recent vaccinations or infective illnesses. She reported hoarseness, but laryngoscopic examination was unremarkable. Neurologic examination showed bilateral loss of the gag reflex; other cranial nerves were intact. There was no neck or limb weakness, sensory examination was normal, and deep tendon reflexes were normal in the arms and mildly decreased in the legs. Initial laboratory studies showed no evidence of inflammation, and ECG was normal. Brain MRI with contrast enhancement revealed no new lesions. On day 6 of illness, a video fluoroscopic swallowing study (VFSS) showed decreased tongue-base retraction, minimal hyolaryngeal excursion, a wide column of contrast in the laryngeal vestibule with silent aspiration (PAS 8), reduced pharyngeal contraction with significant pharyngeal residue, and soft palate elevation impairment causing nasal escape. On day 8, the white blood cell count was 12.79×10^9/L, ESR 41 mm/h, and CRP 2.73 mg/dL. On day 14, repeat VFSS findings were similar; nasogastric tube feeding was instituted due to a 9 kg weight loss over 2 weeks. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck ruled out structural swallowing abnormalities. Chest CT showed aspiration pneumonia, and piperacillin/tazobactam was started. On day 21, she developed watery diarrhea that improved after antibiotics were stopped. Thyroid function tests, tumor markers, acetylcholine receptor and muscle-specific kinase antibodies were unremarkable. Serologic testing did not detect IgG or IgM antibodies against GD1b, GM1, or GQ1b; anti-GT1a antibodies were not available. Serial electrophysiological studies on days 6, 19, and 36—including NCSs, RNS, and needle EMG of bulbar, trunk, and limb muscles—revealed only bilateral median entrapment neuropathy at the wrist and positive sharp waves in thoracic and lumbar paraspinal muscles, without evidence of peripheral neuropathy, myopathy, or neuromuscular junction disorder.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Stroke or encephalitis was considered but deemed unlikely — “Results from brain imaging, electrophysiologic studies (NCS, EMG, and RNS), and laboratory tests collectively indicated a low probability of other conditions, including stroke, encephalitis, peripheral polyneuropathy, myopathy, and neuromuscular junction disorders.”  
2. Structural lesions of the neck and pharynx were excluded — “Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck ruled out structural abnormalities related to swallowing.”  
3. Peripheral polyneuropathy, myopathy, and neuromuscular junction disorders were excluded by electrophysiology — “Serial electrophysiological examinations failed to diagnose any peripheral neuropathy, myopathy, or neuromuscular junction disorder that could explain the patient’s sudden dysphagia.”  
4. Motor neuron disease (e.g., progressive bulbar palsy or ALS) was ruled out despite paraspinal denervation, because there was no craniobulbar denervation — “While denervation of thoracic paraspinal muscles on EMG findings often occurs in patients with motor neuron disease … no denervation potential was observed in the craniobulbar muscles. This ruled out motor neuron diseases such as progressive bulbar palsy or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.”  
5. Myasthenia gravis was excluded by serology — “Antibody tests for myasthenia gravis (acetylcholine receptor antibody and muscle-specific kinase antibody) yielded unremarkable results.”  
6. Alternative antiganglioside-mediated bulbar palsy variants were considered but partially unassessed — “The serological test for antiganglioside antibodies did not detect IgG or IgM antibodies against GD1b, GM1, or GQ1b. However, other antibodies, such as anti-GT1a antibody, were not available for evaluation…”
